[v1.2.0 is out](https://github.com/yoheinakajima/activegraph/releases/tag/v1.2.0) — and yes, it's the FalkorDB release. The `GraphStore` seam, `FalkorDBGraphStore` with native `AGRelation` edges, and the Cypher query push-down all ship, i.e. the full arc from #38/#41/#43/#45 and your PRs #39/#46. Thanks for driving that end-to-end.

A few things that landed around it:

- The architectural decisions are locked in [CONTRACT.md § v1.2](https://github.com/yoheinakajima/activegraph/blob/main/CONTRACT.md) (#1–#6), so the seam's invariants (log is truth, projection is disposable, Python hook defaults define semantics) are now contract, not just code.
- The [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/yoheinakajima/activegraph/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) has migration notes — short version: none needed. The layout change from relations-as-nodes to native edges migrates nothing because the projection re-replays from the event log.
- The test suite is now a CI gate with a `falkordb-embedded` leg, so the `GraphStoreConformance` suite runs on every PR going forward.

`pip install -U 'activegraph[falkordb]'` and you're on it. Closing this one out.

I have developed a local proof-of-concept, complete with execution logs and comprehensive examples. Before proceeding, I want to ensure there are no critical logical pitfalls. If the core concept seems sound, would love to discuss it further.

Confirming this on `main` @ `8aedb18` (Python 3.12.13, Ubuntu 22.04), running
from a source checkout rather than the wheel:

```
same_object_returned: True
in_memory_value: 2
persisted_value:  1
```

Adding a note on why this matters beyond the surprise, in case it helps
prioritise: we are building on the "log is truth" property, and this makes the
log disagree with itself *within a single process* — `graph.events` and the
store return different payloads for the same event id. A reader that trusts the
in-memory log and a reader that trusts SQLite reach different conclusions, with
nothing anywhere marking the divergence.

Our workaround is on the caller side: never retain or mutate a payload after
handing it to `emit`. That is easy to state and hard to enforce across a
codebase, which is why we would rather not carry it indefinitely — if `emit`
deep-copied (or froze) the payload at the boundary, the invariant would hold
without every call site having to remember.

Happy to send a PR if you have a preference between copying at `emit` and
rejecting mutable payloads outright.

## Update

Since posting this, I found and closed a gap in my own accounting: cross-checking all 78 findings against what actually got assigned to an implementation set turned up **19 that had fallen through a planning gap** — never deliberately descoped, just never assigned to any of the 5 fix sets in the first place.

Ran those 19 through the same process (research → TDD plan → independent cold review → plan enhancement → implementation, each stage fresh-context to catch what the previous stage might have missed):

- **15 fixed** with real Red/Green/Refactor test coverage (full suite: 1762 passed / 59 skipped, same single pre-existing unrelated failure as before)
- **3 turned out already fixed** — incidental side effects of the original 53, confirmed by direct re-read of current source rather than trusted from either doc
- **1 blocked on external infrastructure** (a doc-site DNS/Pages dependency, not something an in-repo code change can resolve)

Current total: **71 of the 78** original findings are now fixed and verified (up from 53). The remaining 7: 4 are deliberate "reserved / declared-but-intentionally-inert" design decisions rather than bugs (e.g. `PackPolicy.requires_approval` is owner-attribution metadata, not a write-gate — that's a documented contract clarification, not an oversight), 1 is partially addressed, and the 1 external-infra one above.

Offer's the same as before — happy to open a clean PR (code fixes only, no fork-specific docs/tooling) against current `main` here if useful, share the full updated citation list, or just leave this as a reference. Let me know either way.

Confirmed against `main` at `8aedb18`. This violates the log-as-truth invariant, not just an ownership convention.

The accepted direction is one canonical event-acceptance boundary: normalize through the same JSON adapter in every mode, store a runtime-owned value with no caller aliases, append durably before projection, and return detached values from `emit`, event reads, sinks, and listeners. This is now in the v1.11 Trust Boundary milestone with cross-EventStore conformance coverage. Thank you for the unusually clear reproduction.

Confirmed against `main` at `8aedb18`. The applied/version-advanced record is an integrity defect.

Decision: the patch vocabulary is exactly `update | replace`. Object creation and removal keep their dedicated `object.created` / `object.removed` operations; they do not fit the existing-target optimistic-concurrency contract of a patch. v1.11 will validate before emission, make projector dispatch exhaustive, and diagnose historical applied patches carrying unsupported ops rather than silently assigning them a new meaning. Thanks for identifying the documentation/implementation split precisely.

The shared-run failure is confirmed and is a v1.11 integrity blocker: the losing runtime currently advances in memory before SQLite rejects the append.

One clarification on the second case: logical ids are intentionally scoped to `run_id` (CONTRACT v0.5 #12), so `(run_a, evt_001)` and `(run_b, evt_001)` are distinct durable references and forks deliberately preserve ids. We will keep that property and make it explicit at cross-run boundaries.

The accepted writer model is one logical writer per run, multiple readers, and concurrent writers to different runs. First-party stores will atomically compare an expected run head and raise a typed `ConcurrentWriterError` before projection when another writer won. Recovery is reload under a fresh writer handle, not regenerating an id and interleaving two schedulers. Thank you for surfacing both the operational failure and the ambiguity in how the identity scope is communicated.

Confirmed. The implementation and tests consistently enforce exclusive identifier ownership; the phrase “with different definitions” is the stale part of v0.9 #6.

Decision: keep the fail-closed name/ownership behavior and amend the contract. Equivalent Python objects do not establish safe co-ownership: disable semantics, provenance attribution, schema evolution, and tool/behavior resolution still need one owning pack. Only loading the same `(pack.name, pack.version)` is idempotent. This is assigned to v1.11 and will update all five named categories together, as suggested.

The process-global logging mutation is confirmed in the implementation. I could not reproduce the exact two-test failure under Python 3.11.15 + pytest 9.1.1 (`4 passed` alone; `16 passed` with quickstart first), so the visible failure is runner/version-sensitive, but the isolation defect is real.

v1.11 will address the class rather than patch only these assertions: tests that mutate logging, redactors, registries, or process dedupe state must snapshot/restore it, and in-process CLI helpers must not leave undocumented ambient state behind. The targeted ordering reproduction will remain as a regression where the supported pytest matrix exhibits it.

Promoted into the v1.12 Projection Query Planning milestone together with #64.

The decision is broader than Falkor-specific predicate translation: `Graph` builds a structured object-query plan, a backend consumes only parity-proven clauses, and it returns candidates plus the residual predicate for canonical Python evaluation. FalkorDB may dual-write only explicit per-type top-level scalar index fields into reserved projection properties. The first subset stays narrow (`==`, `!=`, ordered scalar comparisons with missing/`None` parity); nested/container and ambiguous membership semantics remain residual. This issue remains the design/acceptance record for indexed `where` push-down.

Confirmed in the current code, and the supplied evidence is sufficient to treat this as a real scalable-backend gap. Thank you for respecting the contract-first gate and preparing a focused implementation.

This is now the first acceptance slice of v1.12's structured object-query plan rather than a permanently standalone `has_object_of_type` hook. Existence is a result mode: a backend may stop at one row when it consumed all relevant predicates; otherwise canonical residual evaluation continues. The acceptance gate preserves `None`, empty-string, add/remove-last, and backend parity while asserting one returned row and zero payload decodes for the Falkor path. I am implementing the shared plan boundary first so this optimization and #51 do not grow separate semantics.

The operational goals are valid, but `TemporalEventStore` is not an accepted core direction, so I am closing this specific proposal as not planned.

ActiveGraph's EventStore remains the domain log and replay authority. Temporal Workflow History has a different job and incompatible lifecycle constraints (including bounded histories/Continue-As-New and no ActiveGraph truncate/fork semantics). Making either a derivation of the other would create two authorities.

The accepted integration boundary is a separately versioned host adapter: Temporal may schedule runtime quanta, durable approvals, isolated trials, and graph-free `perform` activities while one serialized ActiveGraph writer owns graph `prepare`/`commit`. Activities reference durable idempotent attempts so workflow retry cannot duplicate an external effect. A proof will live outside the runtime package first; any later core seam must be provider-neutral and justified by deployment evidence. Your proof-of-concept may still be useful against that host-layer contract.

This is high-signal work, and I want to absorb it without making the fork an alternative source of runtime law.

Once attached, I will import the integrity/taxonomy/atomicity/resource findings into v1.11 and invite clean contract-first PR batches. Please keep provider additions, repair-pack tooling, and fork architecture out of those batches. The issue stays open as `status: needs-info` until the inventory is available.

I am preparing two minimal runtime bug reports plus a provider/backend architecture proposal, and this structure is very helpful. That repository/PR currently returns 404 both publicly and for the authenticated `TrendpilotAI` account, and it does not appear in the maintainer's public repository list. 1. link a public ADR/record external contributors can read; or
2. state the minimum public architecture context that should be included directly in an RFC until the repository is available?

The rest of the proposed gate is actionable from this PR: owning layer, threatened invariant, failure/recovery model, explicit non-goals, and evidence that would disprove the proposed fix.

### 2. The trusted-contributor carve-out is ambiguous

`CONTRIBUTING.md` preserves direct-PR rights for named trusted contributors, while `TRIAGE.md` says every non-trivial PR links a `status: ready-for-pr` issue and the PR template names only the trivial-fix carve-out. Should a trusted contributor still need a ready issue, or may they write `trusted-contributor carve-out` in the template?

### 3. The template count is stale

`CONTRIBUTING.md` still says to use one of "three templates." This PR would make five structured issue templates: bug, feature, question, architecture, and audit.

I am testing an external backend pattern that puts the authoritative EventStore and disposable GraphStore in one transactional database. PR #78's append-before-project rule is the correct safe default for independent stores, but it exposes one compatibility boundary worth deciding explicitly.

### Reproducible ordering problem

The released v1.10 order is:

```text
apply_event -> GraphStore.put_* stages projection delta
EventStore.append -> commits event + staged delta + projection cursor
```

An external co-located adapter can therefore commit the event and its derived projection delta in one database transaction.

At this PR's current head, the order is:

```text
EventStore.append -> no current delta exists yet
apply_event -> GraphStore.put_* stages the delta after append returns
```

With the same adapter, event N commits the empty or event N-1 buffer, the durable projection remains one event behind, and the final staged delta may never flush. I confirmed the order change directly at `221d9ecd8dcba510c4707c219b463a9a1404efc2`; this is not an argument to restore project-before-append as the default.

### Architecture question

Should the post-v1.11 extension surface reserve an **optional atomic acceptance coordinator** for co-located backends?

A possible shape is:

1. canonicalize and validate the event;
2. prepare its projection delta in an isolated, non-visible overlay;
3. CAS-commit the event, delta, run head, and projection cursor in one backend transaction;
4. publish the accepted in-memory state and offer observers only after commit.

Independent EventStore/GraphStore pairs would keep this PR's append-first behavior unchanged.

### Invariants and gates

- The event remains authoritative; the projection remains replayable and disposable.
- Projection preparation, stale-writer rejection, or commit failure changes neither durable log nor visible projection.
- Success advances event head and projection cursor together.
- Observers see only committed accepted events.
- Replay produces the same projection digest.
- An ambiguous commit result is resolved by reading the canonical event ID and projection cursor: event present/projection behind recovers by replay; projection present without its event is a provider-integrity failure and fails closed.
- A process failure after database commit but before local publication recovers by reload/replay rather than re-accepting a different head.
- No distributed two-phase commit, external-sink atomicity, provider-specific schema, or product behavior enters core.

If this belongs in a separate architecture issue after #78 rather than this release, I will follow that route and wait for `status: ready-for-pr` before proposing code. The immediate goal is to make the compatibility boundary explicit so external adapters do not accidentally depend on call order again.

Thanks for the thorough audit work — really useful.

Triage docs just landed in #80 (invariant-first intake + inventory expectation for broad audits).

Thanks for the LadybugDB suggestion — interested in exploring this.

Could you sketch how it would sit against the GraphStore interface? Specifically: which methods, sync vs async, embed vs client, and any deps/size constraints. Won't commit to shipping until that lands.

Good question — full-replay audit vs branch privacy is a real tension here.

Quick clarifying ask: do you need (a) soft isolation (ACLs on projections), or (b) cryptographic/structural non-leakage under a hostile full dump?

If it's (b), mind opening a design/RFC issue with the threat model so we can reason about it properly?

It's (b). With the full log but no keys, A's raw content never appears.
That's what .me does today, and it's tested. Reconstructing B on replay without A is the open part, and it's the real tension: either B's output is logged as its own event, or replay needs A's key. I'll put together a runnable A/B case and open an RFC with the threat model.

A/B case, running against .me as-is: [<TEST LINK Secret Derivation Replay>](https://github.com/neurons-me/.me/blob/main/Typescript/tests/ActiveGraph/secretDerivationReplay.test.ts)

https://github.com/neurons-me/.me/blob/main/Typescript/tests/ActiveGraph/secretDerivationReplay.test.ts

A is secret under a _ branch, and B = A * 2 is public. With a full dump and no keys, A's raw value never appears, so for A it's (b), structural rather than ACLs. B does replay without keys, because .me logs B's output as a public event and not its formula. The trade-off is that after replay B is a static value and doesn't recompute.

That's the design question I'd compare with ActiveGraph: when a dependent of a private node changes, should the log record its output, its formula, or nothing? I'll open an RFC with the threat model.

  ✓ 1. A under `_`, B public derivation of A (live session)
  ✓ 2. public snapshot + log never contain A raw or the scope key

  ✓ 2c. CURRENT BEHAVIOR: each recompute of B appends a new public memory
  ✓ 3. CURRENT BEHAVIOR: without key, A is absent and B IS available
  ✓ 4. with key: A readable, B present

Whether a value derived from a private node gets logged as its output, its formula, or not at all is exactly what I'd want the RFC to settle, since it decides what replay can reproduce without keys. When you open it, link it here and I'll close this in favor of it.

Building into a fresh store and swapping it in is a good follow-up. Thanks for the acceptance tests; they're going into the fix.

Confirmed on `main` (1.12.0), thanks for the tight repro. Loading an explicit `run_id` that doesn't exist should fail, not create a run. A fix is in progress and will ship in 1.12.1; creating a new run will stay an explicit step.

@TrendpilotAI thanks for raising this, and sorry for the slow reply. You're right that v1.11 changes the ordering co-located backends could lean on: acceptance is now log-first, then projection. Optional atomic acceptance for backends that keep both in one database seems worth supporting, but I'd rather design it on its own than fold it into the trust-boundary change. Please do open the architecture issue you offered and I'll triage it as a design/RFC.

Update: the replay test is now a security test in [.me](https://neurons-me.github.io/.me/docs/Tests), running live in the browser against the published package.

https://neurons-me.github.io/.me/docs/Tests/derived-from-secret.html

Without the key (hydrated snapshot, log replay, wrong key, owner after lock), formulas over the secret don't evaluate and nothing derived leaks into snapshots or logs. The key holder gets the numbers; a formula the owner declares is their disclosure, by design.
